overview: This imported “Germany” label covers 1878 to 1945 but spans three very different governments: the German Empire, Weimar democracy and Nazi dictatorship. Industry, social insurance and city water changed family life; war and hyperinflation brought hardship. Weimar cinemas were lively, while Nazi laws expelled Jewish children from schools and led to genocide and world war. The Nazi state collapsed in 1945, and Germany was occupied and later divided. The people and their histories did not vanish. A separate German Empire card and postwar records tell parts of the same longer story.

periods.title: German Empire and industrial growth
periods.summary: Industrial expansion, insurance and public hygiene changed homes, but income and opportunity were unequal.

periods.title: World War I and collapse of monarchy
periods.summary: War ended the imperial monarchy; revolution opened the way to a republic.

periods.title: Weimar founding and hyperinflation
periods.summary: A democratic constitution began in 1919, while postwar shortages and the 1923 currency crisis devastated savings.

periods.title: Weimar culture and fragile democracy
periods.summary: Cinema and urban culture flourished for some; rural work and class inequality persisted before the republic collapsed.

periods.title: Nazi dictatorship and exclusion
periods.summary: The Nazis destroyed democratic protections and used racist laws to expel Jews from school and civic life.

periods.title: World war, genocide and defeat
periods.summary: Nazi invasion opened war in Europe. The regime and its helpers committed the Holocaust and other mass murders before defeat in 1945.

sections.title: Three regimes under one map label

items.text: The imported map calls 1878-1945 “Germany,” but that label crosses the 1871-1918 Empire, 1918-1933 Weimar Republic and 1933-1945 Nazi dictatorship. These governments were not interchangeable, even when a map uses the same word.

By the turn of the twentieth century, industrial work, social insurance, gas and electricity changed life for some families. Women often took paid work because food costs rose faster than household income. Birth and class still strongly shaped opportunity.

Germ theory turned water and cleanliness into public health questions. New water connections and hygiene campaigns could reduce danger, but a tap or indoor toilet did not arrive in every workers’ room at once.

After World War I the monarchy fell and a republic was founded. The 1919 Weimar constitution said political authority came from the people. This democratic promise had to survive postwar hunger and political conflict.
Hyperinflation in 1923 could make wages and savings lose value at frightening speed. Some people found ingenious ways to manage, but many households lost the security they had worked for.

A family in a city could see a new film at a cinema, while a rural family still worked long days in the fields. Weimar films, including Metropolis, were striking creative achievements; they did not describe every person’s daily life.

A short German sentence from the Weimar civic tradition is “Die Staatsgewalt geht vom Volke aus,” meaning “State authority comes from the people.” It marks the republic’s democratic ideal, not a promise the next regime honored.

sections.title: The Nazi years and their aftermath

items.text: The Nazis took power in 1933 and stripped Jewish neighbors of rights. The 1935 Nuremberg Laws classified people by ancestry. Laws then pushed Jewish children and teachers out of ordinary schools and doctors out of work.

Nazi Germany’s invasion of Poland began European war in 1939. It and its allies and collaborators murdered six million Jewish people in the Holocaust and millions of others. A child’s school lesson about this era should name the victims and the perpetrators, not call it only “a hard time.”

Families lived very different wars: persecution, forced flight, military service, bombardment and resistance were not the same experience. The state’s crimes and the varied choices of people within it must be kept distinct.

After Nazi defeat in May 1945, the United States, Britain, France and Soviet Union held power in separate occupation zones. The regime ended, but German people remained; two German states formed in 1949.

ending.text: This 1878-1945 map label ends with Nazi defeat and Allied occupation, not the disappearance of German people. The German Empire and Weimar Republic had already ended as regimes, and separate East and West states formed in 1949. A reunified federal republic began in 1990.
